PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

Prop 45 could clear hurdles imposed by the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) more quickly, allowing projects such as housing, bridges and clean energy infrastructure to be designated as "essential." That designation sets a one-year limit for environmental reviews and a 270-day deadline for CEQA lawsuits against these projects.
What supporters say: Some environmental lawsuits have resulted in tens of millions of dollars in extra costs for projects.
What opponents say: This could weaken environmental protections for air and water. Some also worry that this could help fast-track the construction of data centers without adequate review.

Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.”

The proposition gives eligible project applicants the option of using the new procedures or existing procedures.

Political action committees funded by technology companies, the state's major utilities and other corporate interests have spent nearly twice as much to pass a ballot measure that would greenlight major development projects with minimal environmental or public review as public interest and labor groups have spent opposing it.
Developers and other corporate interests aim to streamline the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, which requires public agencies to identify, disclose and mitigate a development project's negative impacts on a wide range of environmental resources, including wildlife, air and water quality and tribal cultural resources.
Proposition 45 shifts who determines the scope of environmental review from public agencies and communities to project developers by rewriting the state's foundational environmental law to fast-track major projects.
Supporters of Prop 45, sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, have spent more than $56 million to pass the measure, the most recent state records show.
Opponents, led by a coalition of more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations, have spent close to $30 million to defeat what they say will give polluters a free pass.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Election Day is here.
California voters are set to choose a new governor, vote on all other statewide offices and decide 14 propositions.
Advertisement
For this cycle, voters will also elect their U.S. representative using maps that were redrawn to favor Democrats. Californians adopted Proposition 50, which created maps using redrawn districts targeting five Republicans that in turn affected the boundaries of neighboring districts. The races could help decide the balance of power in Congress.
(See live coverage of Election Day starting at 4 a.m. PT in the video above.)
We'll keep updating this story with the latest information as Election Day unfolds.
What time do polls open and close on Election Day?
All California vote centers open Tuesday at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. for those who wish to vote in person or return their ballot there. Voters can also return their vote-by-mail ballot at secure dropbox locations.
California officials recommended that people who planned to mail their ballot get that done at least a week in advance. Mail must be postmarked on or before Nov. 3 to count.
Where can I find my polling place?
You can find a vote center on the back of your county voter information guide or by clicking here (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/polling-place).
The state is also offering a service where people can text "vote" to 468-683 (GOVOTE) to find their polling place.
‘It was so convenient’: Sacramento County's 92 vote centers are open for the Midterm Election (https://www.kcra.com/article/sacramento-county-vote-centers-open-for-election/74312369)
Get the Facts: Can federal agents be at polling places? What voters should know (https://www.kcra.com/article/get-the-facts-can-federal-agents-be-at-polling-places-what-voters-should-know/74277521)
What to know about the Election Day forecast
A cold front passing through will bring some periods of showers and Sierra snow across Northern California. Scattered showers should reach Sacramento and the surrounding area by late morning. Rain will start in the Foothills before noon. In the Sierra, expect rain and snow showers from midday into the early evening. See the full forecast here (https://www.kcra.com/article/northern-california-election-day-rain-snow-november-3/74313505).
Missed your voter registration date? California offers same-day registration
In California, the deadline to register to vote before an election is 15 days. However, if you miss the deadline, you can cast a ballot provisionally. California law states any voter whose qualifications cannot be immediately verified can cast a ballot provisionally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot.https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot). This process involves comparing the signature of the provisional ballot with the signature on the voter's affidavit of registration to ensure the person is properly registered to vote.
California also allows for same-day registration until 8 p.m. on Election Day. You can sign up for conditional voter registration at your county elections office, or any vote center or polling place in your county.
Track your vote in California
The Secretary of State's Office offers a way for voters to track their ballot online (https://wheresmyballot.sos.ca.gov/). The service allows people to receive updates when their ballot is mailed, received, counted or if an issue comes up. Voters will have the option of email, text or phone call updates.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Election Day is here.
California voters are set to choose a new governor, vote on all other statewide offices and decide 14 propositions.
Advertisement
For this cycle, voters will also elect their U.S. representative using maps that were redrawn to favor Democrats. Californians adopted Proposition 50, which created maps using redrawn districts targeting five Republicans that in turn affected the boundaries of neighboring districts. The races could help decide the balance of power in Congress.
(See live coverage of Election Day starting at 4 a.m. PT in the video above.)
We'll keep updating this story with the latest information as Election Day unfolds.
What time do polls open and close on Election Day?
All California vote centers open Tuesday at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. for those who wish to vote in person or return their ballot there. Voters can also return their vote-by-mail ballot at secure dropbox locations.
California officials recommended that people who planned to mail their ballot get that done at least a week in advance. Mail must be postmarked on or before Nov. 3 to count.
Where can I find my polling place?
You can find a vote center on the back of your county voter information guide or by clicking here (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/polling-place).
The state is also offering a service where people can text "vote" to 468-683 (GOVOTE) to find their polling place.

What to know about the Election Day forecast
A cold front passing through will bring some periods of showers and Sierra snow across Northern California. Scattered showers should reach Sacramento and the surrounding area by late morning. Rain will start in the Foothills before noon. In the Sierra, expect rain and snow showers from midday into the early evening. See the full forecast here (https://www.kcra.com/article/northern-california-election-day-rain-snow-november-3/74313505).
Missed your voter registration date? California offers same-day registration
In California, the deadline to register to vote before an election is 15 days. However, if you miss the deadline, you can cast a ballot provisionally. California law states any voter whose qualifications cannot be immediately verified can cast a ballot provisionally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot.https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot). This process involves comparing the signature of the provisional ballot with the signature on the voter's affidavit of registration to ensure the person is properly registered to vote.
California also allows for same-day registration until 8 p.m. on Election Day. You can sign up for conditional voter registration at your county elections office, or any vote center or polling place in your county.
Track your vote in California
The Secretary of State's Office offers a way for voters to track their ballot online (https://wheresmyballot.sos.ca.gov/). The service allows people to receive updates when their ballot is mailed, received, counted or if an issue comes up. Voters will have the option of email, text or phone call updates.

# Proposition 45
Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects.
Initiative Statute.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.”
Figure 1 lists the types of projects eligible for the new procedures.
The proposition (1) tightens time limits for CEQA review, permits, and court challenges; (2) changes parts of the CEQA review process; and (3) changes the court’s review process for CEQA lawsuits.
The proposition gives eligible project applicants the option of using the new procedures or existing procedures.
...
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures.
For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Election Day is here.
California voters are set to choose a new governor, vote on all other statewide offices and decide 14 propositions.
Advertisement
For this cycle, voters will also elect their U.S. representative using maps that were redrawn to favor Democrats. Californians adopted Proposition 50, which created maps using redrawn districts targeting five Republicans that in turn affected the boundaries of neighboring districts. The races could help decide the balance of power in Congress.
(See live coverage of Election Day starting at 4 a.m. PT in the video above.)
We'll keep updating this story with the latest information as Election Day unfolds.
What time do polls open and close on Election Day?
All California vote centers open Tuesday at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. for those who wish to vote in person or return their ballot there. Voters can also return their vote-by-mail ballot at secure dropbox locations.
California officials recommended that people who planned to mail their ballot get that done at least a week in advance. Mail must be postmarked on or before Nov. 3 to count.
Where can I find my polling place?
You can find a vote center on the back of your county voter information guide or by clicking here (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/polling-place).
The state is also offering a service where people can text "vote" to 468-683 (GOVOTE) to find their polling place.

What to know about the Election Day forecast
A cold front passing through will bring some periods of showers and Sierra snow across Northern California. Scattered showers should reach Sacramento and the surrounding area by late morning. Rain will start in the Foothills before noon. In the Sierra, expect rain and snow showers from midday into the early evening. See the full forecast here (https://www.kcra.com/article/northern-california-election-day-rain-snow-november-3/74313505).
Missed your voter registration date? California offers same-day registration
In California, the deadline to register to vote before an election is 15 days. However, if you miss the deadline, you can cast a ballot provisionally. California law states any voter whose qualifications cannot be immediately verified can cast a ballot provisionally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot.https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot). This process involves comparing the signature of the provisional ballot with the signature on the voter's affidavit of registration to ensure the person is properly registered to vote.
California also allows for same-day registration until 8 p.m. on Election Day. You can sign up for conditional voter registration at your county elections office, or any vote center or polling place in your county.
Track your vote in California
The Secretary of State's Office offers a way for voters to track their ballot online (https://wheresmyballot.sos.ca.gov/). # Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects.
Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure.
But Prop 45 also plunged underwater.
Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots.
Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers.

# Proposition 45: Environmental Review
## Proposition 45: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.
### Summary
Proposition 45 creates a new review process for certain projects defined as “essential.”
The measure sets stricter deadlines for state and local agencies to complete both CEQA and permitting reviews.
It also establishes new deadlines for issuing permits and resolving court challenges.
Eligible applicants could choose these new procedures instead of the existing process.
The process for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) reviews is changed for eligible projects.
Specifically, government agencies must specify all information that an application must contain before it is submitted, limiting their ability to request additional information or project changes later.
Environmental impacts generally would be assessed using laws and standards in place when the application was submitted, rather than allowing agencies to revise review standards based on later changes.
Applicants could develop a single project alternative rather than having the agency develop and consider multiple alternatives.
The measure also limits tribal consultation to federally recognized California tribes and places maximum time limits on comments from the public and other government agencies regarding the project.
The measure also changes the guidelines and process for CEQA lawsuits.

# Proposition 45: Environmental Review
## Proposition 45: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.
### Summary
Proposition 45 creates a new review process for certain projects defined as “essential.”
The measure sets stricter deadlines for state and local agencies to complete both CEQA and permitting reviews.
It also establishes new deadlines for issuing permits and resolving court challenges.
Eligible applicants could choose these new procedures instead of the existing process.
The process for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) reviews is changed for eligible projects.
Specifically, government agencies must specify all information that an application must contain before it is submitted, limiting their ability to request additional information or project changes later.
Environmental impacts generally would be assessed using laws and standards in place when the application was submitted, rather than allowing agencies to revise review standards based on later changes.
Applicants could develop a single project alternative rather than having the agency develop and consider multiple alternatives.
The measure also limits tribal consultation to federally recognized California tribes and places maximum time limits on comments from the public and other government agencies regarding the project.
The measure also changes the guidelines and process for CEQA lawsuits.

## Proposition 45: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.
### Summary
Proposition 45 creates a new review process for certain projects defined as “essential.”
The measure sets stricter deadlines for state and local agencies to complete both CEQA and permitting reviews.
It also establishes new deadlines for issuing permits and resolving court challenges.
Eligible applicants could choose these new procedures instead of the existing process.
The process for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) reviews is changed for eligible projects.
Specifically, government agencies must specify all information that an application must contain before it is submitted, limiting their ability to request additional information or project changes later.
Environmental impacts generally would be assessed using laws and standards in place when the application was submitted, rather than allowing agencies to revise review standards based on later changes.
Applicants could develop a single project alternative rather than having the agency develop and consider multiple alternatives.
The measure also limits tribal consultation to federally recognized California tribes and places maximum time limits on comments from the public and other government agencies regarding the project.
The measure also changes the guidelines and process for CEQA lawsuits.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Election Day is here.
California voters are set to choose a new governor, vote on all other statewide offices and decide 14 propositions.
Advertisement
For this cycle, voters will also elect their U.S. representative using maps that were redrawn to favor Democrats. Californians adopted Proposition 50, which created maps using redrawn districts targeting five Republicans that in turn affected the boundaries of neighboring districts. The races could help decide the balance of power in Congress.
(See live coverage of Election Day starting at 4 a.m. PT in the video above.)
We'll keep updating this story with the latest information as Election Day unfolds.
What time do polls open and close on Election Day?
All California vote centers open Tuesday at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. for those who wish to vote in person or return their ballot there. Voters can also return their vote-by-mail ballot at secure dropbox locations.
California officials recommended that people who planned to mail their ballot get that done at least a week in advance. Mail must be postmarked on or before Nov. 3 to count.
Where can I find my polling place?
You can find a vote center on the back of your county voter information guide or by clicking here (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/polling-place).
The state is also offering a service where people can text "vote" to 468-683 (GOVOTE) to find their polling place.

A cold front passing through will bring some periods of showers and Sierra snow across Northern California. Scattered showers should reach Sacramento and the surrounding area by late morning. Missed your voter registration date? California offers same-day registration
In California, the deadline to register to vote before an election is 15 days. However, if you miss the deadline, you can cast a ballot provisionally. California law states any voter whose qualifications cannot be immediately verified can cast a ballot provisionally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot.https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot). This process involves comparing the signature of the provisional ballot with the signature on the voter's affidavit of registration to ensure the person is properly registered to vote.
California also allows for same-day registration until 8 p.m. on Election Day. You can sign up for conditional voter registration at your county elections office, or any vote center or polling place in your county.
Track your vote in California
The Secretary of State's Office offers a way for voters to track their ballot online (https://wheresmyballot.sos.ca.gov/). # Proposition 45: Environmental Review
## Proposition 45: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.
### Summary
Proposition 45 creates a new review process for certain projects defined as “essential.”
The measure sets stricter deadlines for state and local agencies to complete both CEQA and permitting reviews.
It also establishes new deadlines for issuing permits and resolving court challenges.
Eligible applicants could choose these new procedures instead of the existing process.
The process for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) reviews is changed for eligible projects.
Specifically, government agencies must specify all information that an application must contain before it is submitted, limiting their ability to request additional information or project changes later.
Environmental impacts generally would be assessed using laws and standards in place when the application was submitted, rather than allowing agencies to revise review standards based on later changes.
Applicants could develop a single project alternative rather than having the agency develop and consider multiple alternatives.
The measure also limits tribal consultation to federally recognized California tribes and places maximum time limits on comments from the public and other government agencies regarding the project.
The measure also changes the guidelines and process for CEQA lawsuits.

The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects.
Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure.
But Prop 45 also plunged underwater.
Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots.
Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I'm checking whether the Berkeley IGS poll from October 19–25 included Prop 45, since a California Builders Alliance newsletter cites its tax-related numbers for Props 40 through 43.

I'm going through the remaining polls now, starting with the Probolsky result that has Prop 45 narrowly ahead, and the South Bay Chronicle piece from November 1 that compares two polls on the measure's final weekend. I also want to check whether the October Emerson poll asked about Prop 45 at all.

I'm weighing the Yes side's advantage in funding and its narrow lead in the Probolsky poll against Democratic, labor, and environmental opposition and the common pattern of ballot measures losing ground late in a campaign. Prop 45’s final weekend: two polls, two different answers, and a Bay Area that is the measure’s toughest crowd
PPIC’s October survey has the CEQA overhaul trailing 46% to 50% among likely voters, down from a narrow lead in September. A Probolsky Research poll has it narrowly ahead. Probolsky finds the Bay Area the most skeptical region.
November 1, 2026
Top image: The California State Capitol in Sacramento. Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

**TAKING THE PULSE:** Support for a measure that would roll back elements of the state’s landmark environmental review law is slipping, according to a new poll.
Half of likely voters said they would vote “no” on Proposition 45 if the election had been held on the day they were surveyed, according to a poll the Public Policy Institute of California released on Tuesday night.
Forty-six percent of likely voters said they were a “yes” on the ballot measure, while 4% didn’t know.
A September PPIC poll found that 49% of voters were a yes on Prop 45.
To pass, a majority of votes for the measure will have to be “yes.”
The PPIC interviewed 1,086 likely voters between Oct. 16 and Oct. 22. The organization found that a majority of likely voters in the Los Angeles and Bay Area regions oppose Prop 45, while a majority of voters in the Inland Empire and San Diego regions support it.

Prop 45’s final weekend: two polls, two different answers, and a Bay Area that is the measure’s toughest crowd
PPIC’s October survey has the CEQA overhaul trailing 46% to 50% among likely voters, down from a narrow lead in September. A Probolsky Research poll has it narrowly ahead. Probolsky finds the Bay Area the most skeptical region.
November 1, 2026
Top image: The California State Capitol in Sacramento. Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

Prop 45’s final weekend: two polls, two different answers, and a Bay Area that is the measure’s toughest crowd
PPIC’s October survey has the CEQA overhaul trailing 46% to 50% among likely voters, down from a narrow lead in September. A Probolsky Research poll has it narrowly ahead. Probolsky finds the Bay Area the most skeptical region.
November 1, 2026
Top image: The California State Capitol in Sacramento. Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

Prop 45’s final weekend: two polls, two different answers, and a Bay Area that is the measure’s toughest crowd
PPIC’s October survey has the CEQA overhaul trailing 46% to 50% among likely voters, down from a narrow lead in September. A Probolsky Research poll has it narrowly ahead. Probolsky finds the Bay Area the most skeptical region.
November 1, 2026
Top image: The California State Capitol in Sacramento. Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

Prop 45’s final weekend: two polls, two different answers, and a Bay Area that is the measure’s toughest crowd
PPIC’s October survey has the CEQA overhaul trailing 46% to 50% among likely voters, down from a narrow lead in September. A Probolsky Research poll has it narrowly ahead. Probolsky finds the Bay Area the most skeptical region.
November 1, 2026
Top image: The California State Capitol in Sacramento. Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

I'm going to check whether the Berkeley IGS poll from October 19–25 asked about Prop 45, since a builders' group said it didn't, and look at whether the Emerson poll from October 17–19 has any numbers on it.

I'm going to check whether Newsom has taken a stance on Prop 45 and whether the labor split is shifting, and I'll also look for research on how ballot measures tend to lose support as Election Day approaches.

Proposition 45 is forecast as a environment and energy measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . ### Summary
Proposition 45 began as initiative 25-0023, filed by proponent Kurt Oneto with the California Attorney General’s Office on October 21, 2025.
The initiative was cleared for signature gathering on December 26, 2025.
Supporters submitted signatures in April 2026 and the Secretary of State reported that the minimum signature requirement had been met in June 2026.
The measure therefore qualified for the November 2026 ballot.
Proposition 45 creates a new review process for certain projects defined as “essential.”
The measure sets stricter deadlines for state and local agencies to complete both CEQA and permitting reviews.
It also establishes new deadlines for issuing permits and resolving court challenges.
Eligible applicants could choose these new procedures instead of the existing process.
The process for California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) reviews is changed for eligible projects.
Specifically, government agencies must specify all information that an application must contain before it is submitted, limiting their ability to request additional information or project changes later.
Environmental impacts generally would be assessed using laws and standards in place when the application was submitted, rather than allowing agencies to revise review standards based on later changes.

How this is built
Proposition 45 is forecast as a environment and energy measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. I've got Kalshi putting Prop 45 at about 32% to pass, and I'm trying to reconcile Polymarket, which shows figures anywhere from the low 30s to the 60s depending on which snapshot I'm looking at. Since those readings don't agree, I want a more reliable source, so I'm checking defirate.com's numbers next.

I'm pulling the Polymarket numbers together: the readings run from roughly 31% to 39% depending on the snapshot, and one page shows 50%. Kalshi sits around 32%. The onpointpolitics model puts Prop 45 at about 48%, a toss-up leaning slightly to No, while the markets lean No.

I'm weighing whether the question means "is the Yes side more likely to win," in which case the answer is no because the No side is favored. The wording is ambiguous, though, so I'm checking whether a literal yes or no about "which side" would make more sense.

I'm checking the latest figures to decide whether the question has a clear answer. The election-night date is still in view, so I need to confirm which snapshots are current before settling on a yes or no.

I'm checking whether any results are already indexed past November 3, so I'll search for outcome reports on Prop 45 before settling on a prediction.

I'm checking whether the Yes/No prediction markets and the onpointpolitics model agree, and whether any election results have been indexed yet. The latest pages still show pre-results snapshots, which suggests the index stops around November 2–3. I'll look at how the model handles undecided voters, since that could shift its estimate.

Next I'm checking the funding picture and any late developments, including whether Newsom has taken a position in the final days and where the Los Angeles Times and San Francisco Chronicle editorial boards stand. I also want to see labor's split, since the SEIU opposition and the building trades' possible support for the PLA requirement could matter.

I'm checking whether labor's split and the building trades' stance could shift the outcome. I'm also weighing the base rate for California initiatives that sit under 50% in late polls, which usually fail, though undecided voters occasionally break toward Yes.

I'm looking for research on whether ballot measures lose support as Election Day nears, the so-called "undecided breaks no" pattern, and checking how PPIC's polls have held up on past propositions like Prop 33.

I'm weighing the money picture next: Yes has slightly more spending, but outspending doesn't guarantee passage, and heavily opposed measures often fail. I'm also noting that Democrats largely oppose Prop 45 in a Democratic-leaning electorate, which could push the outcome toward No.

Taking the market prices (roughly 31–39% for Yes) and the model's near-toss-up 47.8%, together with PPIC showing No ahead, the picture points toward No being more likely to win. Yes also looks to be losing ground over the campaign.

I'm settling how to read the question: if it asks whether the Yes side wins, the answer is "no," since the markets, the model, and the polling all lean toward the No side.

I'm weighing the PPIC poll, which shows No ahead 50 to 46, with a seven-point swing toward No in a month. Prediction markets put Yes around 31 to 39 percent, and the model sits near a toss-up at 47.8 percent. Taken together, these point toward No.

I'm weighing the Probolsky numbers, which I can't fully reconcile without the gender split, so I'll set them aside. Overall, the markets at roughly 65–70% No, the PPIC poll trending toward No, and the model's 48% Yes all point toward No. Before settling on an answer, I want to check the onpointpolitics forecast details and Polymarket's current price.

I'm going to check whether the Berkeley IGS poll from October 19–25 asked about Prop 45, since a builders' group said it didn't, and look at whether the Emerson poll from October 17–19 has any numbers on it.

I'm going to check whether Newsom has taken a stance on Prop 45 and whether the labor split is shifting, and I'll also look for research on how ballot measures tend to lose support as Election Day approaches.

Proposition 45 creates a new review process for certain projects defined as “essential.”

I've got Kalshi putting Prop 45 at about 32% to pass, and I'm trying to reconcile Polymarket, which shows figures anywhere from the low 30s to the 60s depending on which snapshot I'm looking at. Since those readings don't agree, I want a more reliable source, so I'm checking defirate.com's numbers next.

I'm pulling the Polymarket numbers together: the readings run from roughly 31% to 39% depending on the snapshot, and one page shows 50%. Kalshi sits around 32%. The onpointpolitics model puts Prop 45 at about 48%, a toss-up leaning slightly to No, while the markets lean No.

I'm weighing whether the question means "is the Yes side more likely to win," in which case the answer is no because the No side is favored. The wording is ambiguous, though, so I'm checking whether a literal yes or no about "which side" would make more sense.

I'm checking the latest figures to decide whether the question has a clear answer. The election-night date is still in view, so I need to confirm which snapshots are current before settling on a yes or no.

I'm checking whether any results are already indexed past November 3, so I'll search for outcome reports on Prop 45 before settling on a prediction.

I'm checking whether the Yes/No prediction markets and the onpointpolitics model agree, and whether any election results have been indexed yet. The latest pages still show pre-results snapshots, which suggests the index stops around November 2–3. I'll look at how the model handles undecided voters, since that could shift its estimate.

Next I'm checking the funding picture and any late developments, including whether Newsom has taken a position in the final days and where the Los Angeles Times and San Francisco Chronicle editorial boards stand. I also want to see labor's split, since the SEIU opposition and the building trades' possible support for the PLA requirement could matter.

I'm checking whether labor's split and the building trades' stance could shift the outcome. I'm also weighing the base rate for California initiatives that sit under 50% in late polls, which usually fail, though undecided voters occasionally break toward Yes.

I'm looking for research on whether ballot measures lose support as Election Day nears, the so-called "undecided breaks no" pattern, and checking how PPIC's polls have held up on past propositions like Prop 33.

I'm weighing the money picture next: Yes has slightly more spending, but outspending doesn't guarantee passage, and heavily opposed measures often fail. I'm also noting that Democrats largely oppose Prop 45 in a Democratic-leaning electorate, which could push the outcome toward No.

Taking the market prices (roughly 31–39% for Yes) and the model's near-toss-up 47.8%, together with PPIC showing No ahead, the picture points toward No being more likely to win. Yes also looks to be losing ground over the campaign.

I'm settling how to read the question: if it asks whether the Yes side wins, the answer is "no," since the markets, the model, and the polling all lean toward the No side.

I'm weighing the PPIC poll, which shows No ahead 50 to 46, with a seven-point swing toward No in a month. Prediction markets put Yes around 31 to 39 percent, and the model sits near a toss-up at 47.8 percent. Taken together, these point toward No.

I'm weighing the Probolsky numbers, which I can't fully reconcile without the gender split, so I'll set them aside. Overall, the markets at roughly 65–70% No, the PPIC poll trending toward No, and the model's 48% Yes all point toward No. Before settling on an answer, I want to check the onpointpolitics forecast details and Polymarket's current price.

I'm going to check whether the Berkeley IGS poll from October 19–25 asked about Prop 45, since a builders' group said it didn't, and look at whether the Emerson poll from October 17–19 has any numbers on it.

I'm going to check whether Newsom has taken a stance on Prop 45 and whether the labor split is shifting, and I'll also look for research on how ballot measures tend to lose support as Election Day approaches.

How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

California’s billionaire tax gets a brutal reality check ahead of Election Day – here’s what bettors expect to pass
Daniel Farr
Updated Thu, October 29, 2026 at 12:00 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.
California's billionaire tax is looking like a long shot, with prediction-market traders betting the controversial measure will go down in flames as voters prepare to decide 14 statewide propositions (https://nypost.com/2026/06/30/us-news/see-the-14-measures-on-californias-november-2026-ballot/) next week.
Kalshi and Polymarket International's displayed markets put several proposals in strong positions, while others, including a voter ID requirement and a mandate for community health clinics, are drawing much lower passage estimates.

content.thinking:
The CalMatters fact check from 2019 lines up with the "No" lean: support for measures usually sags as election day approaches, and Prop 45 slipped from 49-46 in September to 46-50 in October, which fits that pattern. I'm also now checking how PPIC's own polling history on similar questions has trended since 1998.

Now I'm working out the base rate for Yes: PPIC's history on about 80 measures shows support usually falling near election day, averaging around 6.6 points a month. With Yes at 46 in late October, that points toward a final result somewhere around 43 to 45 percent, though the earlier drop from 73 to 49 to 46 is mostly explained by the change in ballot wording.

Yes would need a large shift to win, since only 4% are undecided and Yes is at 46. The Probolsky poll showing a slight Yes lead and the market near 50% suggest it could come down to turnout, but my estimate still leans toward No.

I'm checking the market odds again, comparing the Polymarket and Kalshi figures against the snapshot dates to see whether they've moved since the earlier readings. I want the prices to match the latest data before I settle on an estimate.

I'm going to check whether the market odds are current or still from October, and I'll also look at the LAO analysis, though it's not needed for the forecast. I'm also weighing whether a late "No" ad push or the data center narrative could be shifting opinion, and I'll confirm the source dates on the Defirate and Yahoo pages.

The CalMatters fact check from 2019 lines up with the "No" lean: support for measures usually sags as election day approaches, and Prop 45 slipped from 49-46 in September to 46-50 in October, which fits that pattern. I'm also now checking how PPIC's own polling history on similar questions has trended since 1998.

Now I'm working out the base rate for Yes: PPIC's history on about 80 measures shows support usually falling near election day, averaging around 6.6 points a month. With Yes at 46 in late October, that points toward a final result somewhere around 43 to 45 percent, though the earlier drop from 73 to 49 to 46 is mostly explained by the change in ballot wording.

Yes would need a large shift to win, since only 4% are undecided and Yes is at 46. The Probolsky poll showing a slight Yes lead and the market near 50% suggest it could come down to turnout, but my estimate still leans toward No.

I'm checking the market odds again, comparing the Polymarket and Kalshi figures against the snapshot dates to see whether they've moved since the earlier readings. I want the prices to match the latest data before I settle on an estimate.

I'm going to check whether the market odds are current or still from October, and I'll also look at the LAO analysis, though it's not needed for the forecast. I'm also weighing whether a late "No" ad push or the data center narrative could be shifting opinion, and I'll confirm the source dates on the Defirate and Yahoo pages.
